The running track will be a quarter-mile in length, and on the eastern side will form part of the two hundred and twenty yard straight-away. Inside the track will be the football and lacrosse fields and a grass diamond for baseball. The whole plot is to be surrounded by an eight-foot iron fence, and there will be two entrances, one on Eighth street and the other at the end of River street.

President Sullivan, of the Amateur Athletic Union, has looked over the work so far accomplished, and has expressed his approval of the results. He suggested that the track be modeled after the one now being built for the Jamestown Exposition, which tho more expensive than the ordinary kind, would give better results.

The track will be about twenty feet wide, and will consist of cinders and clay. In its construction there will first be layed a layer of coarse, steam cinders, five inches thick, then one of clay, one inch thick, and on top of this four inches of a mixture of finely screened cinders and clay, in the ratio of two to three. The edges will be built of yellow pine boards, held in place by three-foot posts, four feet apart. The whole track will have a slight inward slope of one inch in twenty feet. Next the pole, in the field, a four inch farm drain will carry off the surface water.

It is true that some of the men are getting into shape on the other teams, but that does not help matters much. As things stand now, there is to be a meet with Rutgers on May 5, only four and one-half weeks distant, and if we expect to make a showing at all, every available man must be on hand to do his best and help others to do their best. So far very little interest has been taken in track and it seems as if a good many have failed to realize that it is a varsity sport; that is, a man may win his letter in it, by winning a first place in an intercollegiate meet. In other words, this year, there is a possibility of twelve men winning their letters, since there are to be twelve events in the Rutgers meet.

A good trainer has been engaged to keep the men in shape and coach them. He will also act as physical director for the lacrosse squad. Starting this Monday, there should be but very few days when the men can not be on the track or practising field events, and it is up to them to see that they get there. The fact that this is the first year we have had a chance to show what we can do in track, should add to the incentive for men to come out.

Fortunately Field Day comes the day of the Junior Show, and on this account, as well as because it will be a sort of a try out for the team men, that day should prove very interesting. Right here is a chance for everyone to help the track team by a large attendance; for the track department only receives its money from the general fund of the Athletic Association and so has considerably less at its disposal than the other varsity departments.

headline: TRACK TEAM'S SUCCESS.
transcription:
The track team started out this season with perhaps the greatest handicap any team can experience, no records of previous teams behind it. While it is true that track has been a sport which Stevens had taken up off and on in previous years, no organized team existed before this season. Work started early in the spring in the shape of cross-country running with the lacrosse team. At first prospects looked bright, but it soon became evident the men who were to form the track team were up against a stiff proposition. The enthusiasm previously shown began to dwindle and many men in college became skeptical whether there was a place for track at Stevens. Three of our best distance men, Cooley, Hansell, and Lippincott were disabled because of illness, and most of the others were busy at lacrosse and baseball. This was the outlook a month before the first and only meet, that with Rutgers.

Here Coach Spring took the men in hand and all credit is certainly due him as well as the men themselves. Field Day was scheduled to take place on April 21, the day of the Junior Show, but due to the poor weather it had to be postponed until April 26.

The games brought out a record number of entries and two college records were broken, while the whole showing was so good that prospects looked much better for the Rutgers meet. The score by classes 1909—19; 1910—45; 1911—51; 1912—20. 1911 won the meet.

This contest came off a week later, on May 5, and proved a surprise to nearly everyone. Almost throughout the meet Stevens broke even with the New Brunswick men, and it was not until near the end of the day that it became certain victory was to go to the Red and Black. At the finish the score was Stevens, 47—Rutgers, 57.

Harris, 1911, won the most points for Stevens and in token of this received a handsome cup from the Scarab Club.

At the Intercollegiates Stevens was represented by Harris, Roscoe and Bell. Both Harris and Roscoe started in the high hurdles while Bell started in the half mile, but none of these men succeeded in getting a place in the finals.

The interscholastic meet held on May 1, was a success in spite of the very adverse weather conditions. The 143 entries in this first venture show the ample interest taken by the various schools and point to a very successful Interscholastic meet next year.

On the whole this year's season shows that there is a place for track at Stevens, especially when it is remembered that track helps the other teams, lacrosse and baseball, by keeping the men in good shape and developing their powers of endurance.

headline: TRACK TEAM'S SUCCESS. — continued

Next year's team should do much better financially, there will be no expenses for the intercollegiate trip as we do not have to send any men. The Rutgers meet will be in New Brunswick and amply covered by the guarantee and we can hope for better weather conditions. Mauger, 1910, is captain. Polhemus, 1910, manager. headline: RUNNERS TRAIN CROSS COUNTRY.
transcription:
Cross-country running is now in full swing, and will continue to take place every Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. About 20 men have come out so far, including lacrosse and trackmen. It is desired that this number be increased. Up to the present time, the men who are best qualified by experience for making the lacrosse team, have failed to show up. It is not known whether it appears to these men that cross-country running is beneath their dignity, or whether pure indifference is the cause.

The fact remains that upperclassmen have not come out for the runs and therefore defeat the object of the management, which is to provide an opportunity for the men to get into good physical shape as early as possible.

The runners meet at Park Ave. and Fourteenth Street, at 4:30 and go across the country up to about Forty-second Street. Five miles are usually covered, three miles of trotting breaking the monotony. By 5:30 the men are back at the Institute.

headline: ATHLETIC GOSSIP.
transcription: Lacrosse, baseball and track men are beginning to get in shape for the spring contests. The lacrosse and track men have been out running very frequently of late and for the most part have signified serious intentions by signing the pledges required by the lacrosse and track management. SOME PROMISING MATERIAL IN 1916

When our long hoped for Gymnasium arrives, our chances for a brilliant season at track will be greatly enhanced. Some basket ball in the winter would certainly be effective as a “wind getter.”

The Annual Sophomore-Freshman Track Meet, the only fall track event was not held until November 6th, and did not call forth an unusual amount of rivalry by any means. headline: THIS SEASON’S TRACK PROSPECTS
transcription:
Coach James P. Sullivan to Whip New Men Into Shape

“JOHNNY” HAYES TO ASSIST NOW AND THEN

With the formal opening of the athletic season at hand comes the call for track candidates and the announcement of the schedule and prospects for the season of 1914. This year's schedule is without a doubt one of the best the “Stute” has ever had. With such a schedule, a good team is absolutely necessary, and that is just what Captain Stretch and Manager Bruns intend to have.

The management has succeeded in securing as coach, Mr. James P. Sullivan, a member of the Olympic team in 1906 and again in 1908, when he won the international mile championship at London.

Since that time he has been in professional athletics, coaching the 14th Reg't track team three years and the McCadden Lyceum team for two years. Mr. Sullivan received his track training under Hirschberg, who at present has charge of the Swedish team. Mr. Sullivan is a personal friend of “Johnny” Hayes of Marathon fame, who has promised to officiate at the home meets and to assist in the coaching from time to time.

This year the coach will be on the field for at least three afternoons a week so that systematic practice can be carried on under his immediate direction.

The prospects for a good team this year are of the best. At present, there are about seven “S” men in college, and considerable material in the two lower classes. Captain Stretch hopes to get a freshman or sophomore to fill Zeiger's place in the dashes and another one for the pole vault. The Freshman-Sophomore meet last fall showed that the Class of 1917 has plenty of good material in it and a number of men who are going to give the Juniors and Seniors a hard run for their positions.

It is up to you, 1917, to come out in your full strength on the first day of practice and stick to it until the last meet is over. Stevens needs every man who can get up on that field, not once or twice a week, but every single day after the season opens.

Regular practice will commence April 15th or earlier depending upon the weather and the condition of the track. When this first practice is called every man who has ever done anything or thinks he can do anything in track should report. On April 22nd will be held the Interclass Meet. This will be the opportunity for Captain Stretch and Coach Sullivan to get a real line on the new men and at the same time for the student body to show that it is back of the team and expecting big things this year.

One week later, April 29th, Stevens will take on New York University at New York. On Friday of the same week the team will travel to New Brunswick to meet our old rivals on “the banks of the old Raritan.”

headline: RUTGERS TAKES TRACK MEET
transcription:
Victorious on Her Own Field to the Tune of 63—49

OUR WEIGHT MEN SHOW UP BEST

After a hard fought battle the Stute track team was defeated at the hands of its old rival, Rutgers, by a score of 63 to 49. Stevens weight men proved to be the best point gainers for the “Old Mill,” scoring 21 points out of a possible 24. Capt. Stretch tucked away ten points, taking firsts in the hammer and discus; Grosso made six with second places in the shot and discus; while Kent put the shot 35 ft. 2 in. for first place.

The rain of the previous day made the track, which consists mostly of the famous New Brunswick red clay, very heavy; and a coating of this clay became so thick on the contestants shoes that spikes proved of little use. Coach Sullivan thought the time remarkably fast considering the weather conditions.

In one of the closest contested races of the day Hoinkis, who was in fine form, defeated Segur in the high hurdles, winning for Stevens her only first place in the track events. On the other hand we came in second in every track event, with the exception of the high hurdles and the half mile.

In the sprints Savale was greatly handicapped by the mud as he was also taking Scheuneman's place in the broad jump; but he made Reed, the Rutgers star, extend himself to the utmost to win. Savale finished an easy second in the hundred and the two-twenty. Boyd made a game fight for the four-forty, but Abt, who took the lead at the start, could not be passed.

In the distances Rutgers took first places by a good margin; but the fight for second places in the events led to some of the hottest fights of the day. Hillman, in the mile, came up from behind and in a spectacular sprint passed Wilkins less than ten yards from the tape. In the two mile Stovall, Sharp and Howell kept at each other's heels until within a hundred yards of the finish, when Howell pulled away from his rival with apparent ease.

The judges made one of the closests decisions of the day when they awarded Thompson the broad jump by 20 ft. 5 in. over Campbell 20 ft. 4½ in.

The high jump and pole vault proved to be a Waterloo for the Red and Gray, Rutgers taking both places in these events. Lukens made a desperate attempt to break the Rutgers' high jump record of 5 ft. 9 in., but failed to clear it at that heighth, 5 ft. 7½ in. being his best jump.

Savale, '17, was the highest individual point winner, having 11 to his credit, while Moonan and Frey of C. C. N. Y. were tied with scores of 10 points each.

The track was in excellent condition considering the rainy weather of the past few days. In the hundred Savale pushed Moonan hard for first, the time being 10 3-5 sec.

Hoinkis, the only Stevens entry, won the 120 high hurdles with ease, one C. C. N. Y. man dropping out at the start and the other being disqualified. Moonan, C. C. N. Y., annexed his second first in the 440, crossing the tape ten yards in the lead of Boyd.

Frey broke the C. C. N. Y. record for the mile run by covering the distance in 4 min. 39 4-5 sec. This is 12 3-5 sec. better than the Stevens record for the same distance. Howell finished but did not get a place.

Hoinkis lead across the tape in the 220 hurdles but was disqualified on account of jumping outside of his own lane, race going to P. P. Smith, Jr., '15, Stevens. Lehman, C. C. N. Y., was awarded second.

Hillman surprised himself by lowering his own record for the two-mile to 10 min. 48 3-5 sec., beating Scarlatta of C. C. N. Y. by eight yards.

The 220-yd. dash was particularly exciting, all the contestants displaying lots of speed and although Savale held the lead from the start the result was uncertain, Greenbaum running him a close second and almost tieing him for first.

Thompson, '15, and Scheuneman, '16, showed up well in the running broad. The latter, although not getting a place, gave evidence of improvement over his previous work.

Despite the fact that one of the C. C. N. Y. men remarked that Grosso looked old and possibly might be a professor, he managed to put the shot for 33 ft. 8¼ in.

Stretch had no serious competition in his event and, although handicapped by a wet and slippery field, hurled the hammer a distance of 126 ft. 3 in., which was but 8½ in. short of his own and the Stevens record.

“Shorty” Conard, '15, Stevens, and Hayes of C. C. N. Y., tied for first place in the high jump with the bar at 5 ft. ¼ in. The points were divided equally.

With the bar at 8 ft. ⅝ in. Hoinkis dropped out of the pole vault and Drake, of C. C. N. Y., did not try to go higher.

The appended score shows that the team is well balanced and that it may be expected to win points consistently.

headline: TRACK PROSPECTS VERY BRIGHT

INTERSCHOLASTIC MEET ON MAY 1st

Stevens is about to enter on what should be her most successful track season. The dual meets will be C. C. N. Y. on the 5th of May; Lehigh on the 12th of May; N. Y. U. on the 22nd of May and Rutgers the next Saturday, the 29th. On May 15th, a delegation will be sent to the Middle States Intercollegiates at Haverford, a meet which is attracting more public interest each year.

One of the big events of the season will be the Sixth Annual Interscholastic Track Meet, which will be held on May 1st. The meet has been gradually growing in magnitude and last year attracted two hundred and forty contestants. We have every prospect of even a greater number of entries this year. Nearly every school within a radius of seventy-five miles of New York will be represented this year and a few teams will come much farther. It is in fact, one of the few meets in which the local track men may compete with men who have to travel quite a distance and it was one of these schools, Mercersburg Academy, that won the point trophy last year. headline: RELAY TEAM GETS SECOND PLACE
transcription:
The Varsity Team Makes Excellent Showing at Philadelphia

FRESHMEN GET FOURTH PLACE

Stevens athletics received a big boost last Saturday when our relay team went down to Philadelphia to compete in the Penn relays and captured second place in their class. However it was pretty hard to see our rivals C. C. N. Y. take first place. The Freshmen team also did nobly capturing fourth place against, Yale, Penn and Columbia. As this is our first attempt in one of the classics of the athletic world we can feel very proud of our relay teams.

The first lap of the varsity relay was run by Mesloh who opened up a lead of eight yards. Oetting ran in good style and touched off Captain Hoinkis with a lead of five yards. But Hoinkis was passed just as he made the last turn into the home stretch. He managed to touch Balko our anchor man, off about even. But Balko was running against a very fast man and did well to finish a very close second. As a reward each fellow received a large silver loving cup. The winning time was 3:35:3 made by C. C. N. Y., while our time was 3:39. This is remarkable in that not once during practice did our team come anywhere near that time.

The unlimited Freshmen event came off about an hour after the varsity race. This was very fast, our Freshmen being completely outclassed, two of the men having already run in the varsity race. McQueeney ran first, with Marshall second, Balko running third and Mesloh running fourth, managed to close up the gap and secured fourth place about five yards behind Columbia. Yale won the race in 3:28 with Penn. and Columbia running second and third.

headline: TRACK MEET EASY VICTORY
transcription:
C. C. N. Y. Overwhelmed In First Dual Meet by Score Of 75-37

STEVENS' STRONG IN FIELD EVENTS

The C. C. N. Y. track team travelled to Hoboken last Wednesday May 5th, for their annual defeat. Only this year, the score was a little bit more overwhelming, the count showing 75-37. In seven of the fourteen events the C. C. N. Y. team failed to score a point, our boys finishing one, two.

Despite the fact that the score was one sided, many events created a good bit of interest. The very first event, the 100-yard dash, was as close as any one would want to see; Moonan, one of our visitors being given the decision over Mesloh. Mesloh, however, evened it up by winning the 220, leading Balko also a Stevens man over the tape.

The 440 was one of the best of the day. Balko managed to stay with Breims for almost an entire lap, the two running together like a team of horses and measuring stride for stride. But in the home stretch, Breims passed him and Moonan coming fast managed to beat out Balko at the tape for second.

The mile run furnished plenty of amusement for the spectators. A C. C. N. Y. man started at a rate that would have done John Paul Jones credit, and as the laps increased, he seemed able to hold the big lead and it looked as though he was going to have the last laugh, but he finally broke down with about ¾ of a lap to go and Howell won with Rogers second. Incidently Howell ran the fastest mile of his career and only six seconds behind the Stevens record.

The field events saw Stevens get 40 out of a possible 48 points. Altort managed to beat Phelps by ½ inch in the broad jump although it apparently looked as though Phelps had jumped further. Rudnick managed to get the other 3 points when he got second in the shot. Stretch as usual grabbed both the hammer and discus. However, Grosso gave him a “run for his money” in the discus.

Things look bright for a successful track season.

headline: TRACK MEN TAKE NOTICE
transcription:
Opening is Offered to New Men to Replace Those Lost By Graduation

HAND IN YOUR NAMES AND EVENTS NOW

The first call for track men for the season of 1916 was made by manager Jones last Monday, March 6th. About thirty men appeared at the meeting.

Track seems to be considered a minor sport here at Stevens and does not get the support from the student body that it should. In many colleges it is next in order to football and there is no reason why it should be regarded so lightly here. Track offers an excellent field for a man who is not physically able or cannot spare the time for the other sports to earn his “S.” A man can win his numerals in track during any one of the four years, a thing impossible in any other sport.

This year is an exceptional one for a new man to make the team as practically all the good men of last year were lost by graduation. Men are especially needed in the weights, jumps and distance events. No man knows what he can do in track until he gets out and tries. The secret in track is practice. One of the most notable examples of what can be done is that of John Paul Jones the famous Cornell miler and former record holder, who being on the verge of consumption was urged by his physician to try running and outdoor exercise. He not only restored his health but made himself famous on the track.

The schedule this year is one that the men will like, all the meets being away from home. This means a good time for the fellows that make the team and a good chance to see what other colleges are like. Trips will be made to Lafayette, Lehigh, N. Y. U., Rutgers and the Penn. Relays.

Practice will start at the Savannah yards as soon as the weather permits, so hand in your name with your event at once to Capt. Hoinkis, or Mgr. Jones; watch the bulletin board, and be prepared for practice when the time comes.

The Interclass meet this spring will be a handicap affair, in which every man will have an equal chance to win a place. headline: TRACK TEAM HAS FAIR SEASON
transcription:
Win No Meets but Develop Consistent Winners Who Better Stevens Records

MESLOH IS MIDDLE STATES 220 CHAMPION

The Varsity track team finished a strenuous schedule on Decoration day with a defeat by Lafayette, against whom the Stute was able to register but 27½ points.

Although the team has not won a meet this season it has succeeded in holding down the score of the opposing teams and making them fight hard for every point they tallied.

In the Middle States Intercollegiates the men made an especially fine showing. Mesloh after running a series of trials and semi-finals broke the tape in the 220 yard dash a winner by two yards in a time equalling the Stevens record. Gennert '19, captured second place in the hammer and incidentally, during the season, raised the Stute record in that event by over ten feet. Captain Hoinkis, '16, finished third in the hurdles in the same meet while Phelps, '18, secured fourth in the broad and Roberts '19, tied for the same position, in his specialty, the high jump. In all they tallied 11½ points.

Coach McGall, '07, to whom in a large measure much of the success is due, will return next year and he plans to start practice as soon as college opens in the fall.

Since the building of the Gym several prominent Prep School track men have announced their intention of coming here, while from this year's team the only man lost by graduation will be Captain Hoinkis and with a little more work Phelps should be able to partially replace him in the hurdles.

headline: TRACK TEAM NEEDS MEN
transcription:
Manager Savoye of the track team is out gunning for men. Coach McGall and Dr. Davis are right with him in his hunt. The team does need men. Last year they scored 11½ points in the Middle-States intercollegiate meet and this year it is their ambition to do better. The management has arranged an attractive schedule and is anxious to carry off some of the dual meets but in order to do this the team must have more men. Especially in the field events; weight men particularly are needed. Gennert who could always be relied on to score in these events last season did not return to school this season and his absence leaves a big gap in the team which it is up to some one to fill. Men, too, are needed in the distance runs and in the hurdles, and there is not a single other event in which a place for a consistent man cannot be found.

Men are reminded that they can elect track work as their specialty in the physical training course. Fifteen minutes of each period will be devoted to the sports chosen by the men themselves and track work should appeal to nearly every one. Speak to Dr. Davis to-day rather than wait to be assigned to a sport you will not enjoy. If the sport appeals to you spend a few fifteen minute periods after school besides your regular gym hours.

The season will open, contrary to our usual custom, with a dual meet with Rutgers on April 21, so that there will be little time left to get in shape when the field is opened. Therefore, every man must start now to condition himself. Fifteen minutes everyday will have you in fine shape, but it must be every day.

The team was to have entered a relay in the Brooklyn College games Saturday night but owing to Oetting's services being required on the basketball team, it was decided to withdraw the men at the last minute. The team will however enter in the Penn Relays on April 27-8 and the chances for a win in our class are better than ever before, so good in fact that if enough were to turn out two teams will be entered.

headline: TRACK TEAM IN SECOND PLACE
transcription:
With but 8 Men They Score 18 Points in Jersey City College Games

MESLOH TAKES SIXTY AND ROBERTS THE HIGH

The track team journeyed to Jersey City last Saturday, made their debut on the boards and by taking two firsts, two seconds and one third against the pick of stars from the smaller colleges, took second place in the annual games of the Jersey City College held in the armory there.

The Stevens men entered the rather small team of 8 men and their total of 18 points was a very creditable showing as Fordham, who won the meet with 31, brought over a team of over 40 men. C. C. N. Y. trailed the Stute men close by gathering 17 points and annexing third place.

Mesloh, '18, and Roberts, '19, were the stars of the meet. Mesloh took the 60 in the very good time of 6.1 while Roberts cleared 5 ft. 5 in. in the high jump. Bloss proved to be a fit running mate to Mesloh by taking second place in the 60. Captain Rogers showed some fine form by romping home third in the mile.

The Stevens team was forced to trail Fordham in the mile relay. Bloss got off with a poor start and owing to bad running conditions was not able to pick up much ground. He touched Oetting off in third position and Phil by steady plugging drew up into second place where Peter relieved him of his task. Pete ran a pretty race notwithstanding the fact that he was tired from the 300 and touched Mesloh off in second place, having picked up ten yards. Bill started about 15 yards in the rear of the Fordham man and although he gained perceptibly and covered the quarter in the fast time of 51, he was unable to head off the New Yorker.

Taking the meet as a whole, the Stevens team performed wonderfully well. The Stute men averaged 2.5 points per man, while the New Yorkers averaged but 0.7. However, although the Fordham men presented a few stars, they brought over a big team and made sure of the minor places. The Stute team with a few more men would undoubtedly have trailed the New Yorkers closely. The coaches are anxious to secure more men to balance up the team before the outdoor season opens and the showing of those already out should encourage others to try for the vacancies. Men are especially needed for the field and weight events.

Phelps and Lofquist cleaned up the broad jumps, 21 ft. ½ inch being a bit too far for Rutgers. Piquet managed to get second in the quarter, closely contested by Baggaley. In a bitter race with West Virginia University, our Track team missed first, but got a good second, at the Penn Relays Saturday we being twenty yards ahead of the third team. Eight teams were entered in the event, but six showed up, including New York Law, Dubuque College, Drexel Institute, Jersey City College, and our aforementioned friends from West Virginia.

Bloss started off for us and kept his place with the first man till thirty yards from home, when West Virginia opened throttle and came in five or six yards ahead. Bloss handed the broom stick to Piquet who tried to pull up to first, but did not succeed, giving the stick to Oetting for a second place, Oetting gained a few yards, giving Mesloh, the anchor man, a fair second position. Bill, however, was up against a tough proposition and could only give us a good second, leading Temple University by twenty yards.

Our track record so far has been something to be proud of, getting second in the Indoor Champs, Rutgers's meet, and Penn Relays. Next week we meet C. C. N. Y.

headline: TRACK TEAM AT PENN. RELAYS

Last Saturday the annual Penn. Relays were held at Franklin Field, Philadelphia.

We entered a team in a one mile relay but the horseshoe was lost on the way down to Philadelphia and after the race the men were unable to sport cups. The men composing the team were Mesloh, '19, Bloss, '20, Cornetta, '20, and Ellis, '20, and while they did not come through as winners they deserve credit for their efforts.

headline: STEVENS WINS TRACK MEET
transcription:
Team Travels To New York And Returns Triumphant

Final Score, 62—50

MESLOH AND ROBERTS STAR FOR STEVENS

Last Saturday a dozen of our track athletes took a trip into the wilds of the Bronx and brought home the scalp of a certain N. Y. U. The meet was closely contested and good times were made despite a very heavy track. Cornetta clipped a fifth of a second off our record for the half mile when he did it in 2 minutes 5 4-5 seconds, he also won the mile. Bill Mesloh won three firsts, the 100-yard dash, 120-yard dash and 220-yard low hurdles, doing them all in fast time. Perry Roberts took point honors by winning the 120-yard high hurdles and pole vault and taking second in the high jump and 220-yard low hurdles. Johnny Flockhardt finished first in the discus and hammer and second in the shot. Len Bloss won the broad jump and came in second in the quarter mile.

There was plenty of excitement furnished. The 100-yd., 220-yd., 440-yd. dashes and the high jump and high hurdles were especially close. Owing to a misunderstanding between the judges of the finish in the 220-yd. low hurdles both picked first place and consequently there was no one to pick second. Mesloh was easily first, but second was very close, some said it was a tie, others declared N. Y. U. the winner and one N. Y. U. man said he thought Stevens was the winner. Roberts, who was the cause of all the trouble, had already done the high jump, high hurdles and broad jump and still had the pole vault to do, did not want to run the race over again as N. Y. U. insisted we do, their man being comparatively fresh. We were willing to split the points, but at that time the Stute had only a narrow margin and it looked as if that second place might decide the meet. Finally a coin was tossed, N. Y. U. winning, so that the race was run over again, Roberts easily beating his adversary and with his first in the pole vault winning the meet by the score of 62 to 50.

May 25, the last day of exams, you will have the first chance in years to see your track athletes in a dual meet on their own grounds. There will be a double header with C. C. N. Y., a baseball game and a track meet. Tell “her” to keep that date open, Saturday, May 25.

headline: STEVENS BEATS PRATT
transcription:
Interesting Meet Won By Stute By 46—36

Before a large crowd of interested men, and a representative here and there of the fair sex, the Stevens Track team beat Pratt to the tune of 46 to 36 in the Gym Saturday, February 8. Those present witnessed a fine exhibition of running and jumping and a closely contested meet.

Captain Perry Roberts, “Bill” Mesloh, and Brown starred for the Stute. Clark of Pratt scored the greatest number of points, 18, or one half of Pratt's score.

Roberts won the high jump and the hurdle race, Mesloh took first in the 220 and second in the 25-yard dash. Brown, a freshman, after winning the half in fast time, won the mile in the exceptionally good time of 4 minutes and 48 3-5 seconds. Conrow and Mattimore came in first and second in the 440 with only a fraction of a second's difference in time. In the final event, the relay race in which each man ran two laps on the track, Mesloh, McCrea, Bloss, and Mattimore gained nearly a half a lap on the Pratt team. The average time for each man was 21 3-5 seconds which is very fast, taking into account loss in speed due to passing the baton from one man to the next.

The results of the meet show that the Stute will have a track team that will bring a name to Stevens never owned before in the line of athletics. A glance at the results below will show that weight men are badly needed. Here is a fine chance for a “husky” to win his “S”. Come out and learn how to throw the weights. Al McGall is out coaching the team every afternoon and wants to see a good crowd of weight men show up to learn the art of “putting it across.”

Following is the summary:

- 25-yard dash—won by Clark, Pratt, Mesloh, Stevens.
- 220-yard dash—won by Mesloh, Stevens, McCrea, Stevens.
- 440-yd dash—won by Conrow St., Mattimore, Stevens.

- Mile run—won by Brown, Stevens, King, Pratt.
- Hurdles—won by Roberts, Stevens, Fresinger, Pratt.

The greatest interest is being displayed in these relays since for the first time in three years practically every college in the country is to be represented. headline: STUTE LOSES E. I. A. A. TRACK MEET
transcription:
Bloss Pulls Tendon While Leading Field in 220 Yard Dash

STEVENS FINISHES IN SECOND PLACE

Colgate University won the first annual track meet of the Eastern Intercollegiate Athletic Association May 10th, by a margin of one point over Stevens. Colgate scored 25 points, Stevens 24, and New Hampshire State 21½, in a remarkably close meet for the combination of colleges entered.

Until the last few events New Hampshire State looked like the second place team, but Stevens had things her own way in the field events and managed to nose out ahead of the Granite State team. Bloss was leading the field in the 220 yard dash when he strained a tendon in his left leg and was forced to drop out. The Stute, judging from the records, would undoubtedly have won both the 220 and the running broad jump if this unfortunate accident had not occurred to our star sprinter. This would have meant the winning of the meet by a safe margin.

Rain fell all day long and made fast time on the track extremely difficult. All events, however, were closely contested and margins for the winners were small. Points were well distributed, but Colgate had the advantage of a well balanced team.

Roberts of Stevens, Gillo of Colgate, Driscoll, Boston College, and Nightingale of New Hampshire were conspicuous performers. Nine colleges had teams on the field and there were points for all.

headline: ALL OUT FOR CROSS COUNTRY
transcription:
The firm foundation on which Cornell annually builds a winning track team, is cross country running. All men are urged to come out and run with the team. If you have never done anything in this field come out and try; if you have been running come out again.

We will have on our schedule two dual meets and the Middle Atlantic Championships which will probably be held in Newark. We will have a weekly handicap and a class team championship, members of the winning team to receive numerals.

Then during the winter the track coach will be able to carry on development work and in the spring Stevens will have a better track team.

Any boy with two legs and a backbone is able to run and practice and the never-say-die spirit makes for success.

Now is also the time to begin pole vaulting and practice in all form events, shot, discus, javelin, hurdles, high jumping and broad jumping.

The coach will give advice at any time and will be pleased to have a dozen men come out to learn pole vaulting. We are weak in this event, but it is promised that one of the dozen will break our Stevens record which is not very good.

Mr. McGall urges anyone to come out who wants to do something worth while for his college and for himself. The patience, persistence and courage required of a man all add to that most important part of man's education, the development of his character.

The coach requests that no alibis along the following lines be submitted:—

“I have no wind.”

“I never did anything like this.”

“I am too heavy,”

“I am not heavy enough.”

“I have no time,”

and so on.—

He says he has heard everyone of these and some more, adds that he will tell a man whether he will be able to do anything and if the case is hopeless will recommend the necessary treatment.
summary: An extended appeal by coach Al McGall launches Stevens' first cross country program, announcing two dual meets and the Middle Atlantic Championships on the schedule.

headline: CROSS-COUNTRY MEN ACTIVE
transcription:
A large number of harriers and future harriers answered Coach McGall's call, and appeared on the field ready for work last week. There's still room, however, for as many aspirants as want to come out. Practice started with only two or three laps a day. Now six to eight laps constitute a day's work. Al McGall, '07, is a Stevens graduate who has been coaching successfully at Stevens since 1915. This year with the co-operation of the men, he is introducing this new sport, cross-country. Judging from past observations, he will make the team a success.

J. C. Nicoll, Secretary of the Interfraternity Council, gave a brief resume of the rules governing fraternal rushing which rules will be found on page 130 of the handbook and should be read. Nicoll also spoke for cross-country and showed the possibilities of this sport. You may not be heavy enough for football, or agile enough for basketball, but practice can stretch your legs and develop your muscles, and presto!—a cross-country man.

What Doc Davis says, goes! So when he declares that cross-country running is a good preliminary training for any sport, he must mean it and it must be so. But doesn't that mean something to you? Practice started last week. Al McGall, our veteran track coach, is at the Gym to look you over—all you have to do is come up to see him. We are going to have a good hill and dale schedule; we ought to have a good team. We need more men—how about you?

The announcement of the Intercollegiate A. A. A. A., that it is to resume its cross-country run, which will be held on one of the courses near New York City, will bring a great revival of interest in this sport.

Did you notice that Perry Roberts, '19, representing the N. Y. A. C., placed in the New York A. C. games held recently? Perry took third in the 120 Yard High Hurdles and second in the Pole Vault Handicap with a ten foot jump. He is keeping up the good work—we're all with you, Perry!

headline: STEVENS DROPS CROSS COUNTRY
meet_or_event: Central High School of Newark dual meet; Rutgers dual meet
transcription:
Poor Course To Practice On Given As Reason For Withdrawing

TEAM WAS ENGAGED IN TWO MEETS

Cross Country has been abandoned for the season. “Doc” Davis' opinion that the fellows are young for the sport, and the lack of a proper course to practice on are given as reasons for the decision to disband the team. Track practice in preparation for the indoor season has been substituted for hill and dale sport.

Out of the large squad that replied to the call for hill-and-dalers, Brown, Nicoll, Arlt, Walters, Duguid, Hill, Barnett, and Woodward were chosen as the most promising men. Brown generally led the pack in practice and in two meets that were held he was the first Stevens man to finish.

The first meet was hastily arranged with Central High School of Newark and was held October 18th, on the course around the Castle. Central won by the score of 24 to 32. Brown crossed the tape in the fourth position. The Central team has a reputation for winning high school championships, and the close fight indicated that the Stute was shaping up well.

In the next meet which was held October 25th with Rutgers, over the four and a half mile Branch Brook course in Newark, the Stute did not make a good showing. Rutgers won by the score of 18 to 43, and with the time of 25:34. As usual, Brown finished in the fourth place, and the second Stute man was Arlt, a freshman, who finished in the sixth place. Arlt has come up well lately and should star for the Stute on track. The poor showing of the team was due to minor disabilities. Nicoll and Woodward had foot trouble. The team was furnished with old shoes that had to be tied up with adhesive tape to keep them from falling to pieces. Brown, especially, had an old pair of track shoes, not at all suitable for the hill and dale sport. He had to cut out the spikes, and consequently ran in the race with the soles full of holes.
summary: Despite having just been adopted as a minor sport, cross country was abandoned for the season after losses to Central High School of Newark and Rutgers, citing the runners' youth, a poor practice course, and inadequate equipment.
notability_note: Reports the abandonment of the cross-country program only weeks after it was formally adopted as a minor sport, following two competitive meets.

transcription:
Cross country is abandoned! “Good”, some one says! But, why? It is well that the sport has been dropped, for it is evident that the men who came out were not old enough to run the regular collegiate six miles. The men that replied to Coach McGall's call were nearly all from the Soph and Frosh classes, men who, perhaps, were accustomed to the high school three miles—not the collegiate six. Furthermore, the team had no suitable course over which to practice for the gruelling run. Also, cross country was given no support and little encouragement from the A. A. The equipment was nil; and no team can do good work without proper equipment. So, there was nothing else to do but abandon the sport!

Nevertheless, the men deserve due credit for coming out the way they did. Twenty-five responded to the first call for candidates and were soon put to work. The best of the new men were Arlt, Duguid and Walters, all young men. Brown and Jit Nicoll were the only older men on the job. All worked hard and, mind you, under poor conditions as to course and equipment.

This is a new sport at Stevens. Next year, mayhap, we will be able to do much better!

At any rate cross country was certainly well worth beginning for, as Al McGall has said, cross country is the firm foundation upon which Cornell annually builds a winning track team. Our men are now having track practice on every Monday and Thursday. And Al hasn't all the men he would like to have, either! That means that you should think it over—how about coming out? You hesitate! Why? Al can handle beginners just as ably as vets—all you have to do is report. Simple enough! Why not try it?
summary: An editorial reflects on the abandoned cross-country season, attributing it to young runners, poor facilities, and lack of A.A. support, while expressing hope for a better effort next year and pivoting to a track-practice recruiting pitch.
